lesson_title: Three Highs, One Hairdryer: The Cells That Run SA's Weather
hook_text: Mid-thirties in East London. In July. Meet the hairdryer wind your geography course calls a berg wind.
clip_script: Through winter the inside guard stacks air on the plateau, roughly a kilometre and a half above the sea. When a passing system tugs the pressure down at the coast, that stacked air breaks loose and pours over the escarpment edge, falling toward the shore. Falling air gets squeezed, and squeezed air heats: close to one degree gained for every hundred metres dropped. Fall fifteen hundred metres and the parcel lands about fourteen degrees hotter than it started — a scorching, utterly dry, gusty wind blowing from the land out to sea. That is the berg wind, the mountain wind: the reason East London can post a July afternoon in the mid-thirties while the plateau it came from sits near freezing.
visual_style: Animated cross-section: cool air stacked on the plateau, then an arrow plunging down the escarpment with a rising thermometer overlay, ending on a windswept beach under a red fire-danger flag.
mood: Curious and slightly ominous, building to an aha payoff.
pacing: Steady build down the escarpment, temperature counter ticking upward, hard landing on the fire-danger flag.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and connect all three highs to the wind on your own doorstep.
